page: Amazon Web Services c5a.4xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by the Nitro hypervisor. It features an AMD EPYC 7R32 processor based on the x86_64 architecture, providing 16 dedicated virtual CPUs (8 physical cores with 2 threads per core) running at a clock speed of 3.3 GHz. The CPU includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache. It supports hardware-level features such as AVX, AES, and SHA_NI cryptography extensions. The instance is configured with 32.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, yielding a resource density of 2.0 GB of RAM per core. There is no bundled local storage or GPU hardware. Network connectivity is established with a baseline bandwidth of 5 Gbps.

Benchmark evaluations indicate a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The single-core CPU performance measured via stress-ng falls in the bottom 10 percent, and large-block memory bandwidth (both read and write) is weak, placing in the bottom 25 percent with 37.14 GB/sec and 22.42 GB/sec respectively. However, multi-core CPU performance and cached small-block memory read bandwidth (800.68 GB/sec) perform at an average level. General compute benchmarks, including Geekbench multi-core (7998.0) and Passmark CPU (19648.81), align with the middle 50 percent of tested instances. The instance also exhibits average performance in text processing, software compilation, and static web serving throughput (7.6 GB/sec).

Given the dedicated AMD EPYC processor cores and a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, the c5a.4xlarge offers a balanced compute-to-memory profile for multi-threaded workloads that do not require high single-core speeds or local NVMe storage. It is suitable for tasks such as multi-threaded decompression, software compilation, static web serving, and moderate database operations. For machine learning, it supports small-model LLM inference at average speeds but exhibits weak performance on larger 7B models. The absence of bundled storage and GPUs positions this instance as a cost-efficient option for compute-heavy workloads relying on network-attached storage.
